Depicted in reliefs at Ramesses III's mortuary temple, this mysterious maritime confederation was long blamed for Late Bronze Age raids on Egypt around 1200 BC, though scholars now see them more as a symptom of the era's collapse than its cause. Who were they?
Sea Peoples: Purported ancient tribal confederation of the Late Bronze Age.
Serving five separate terms as prime minister between 1995 and 2022, this long-time Nepali Congress leader saw his tenure dogged by accusations of nepotism and corruption — who is he?
Founded in Japan in 1930 and rooted in the teachings of the 13th-century monk Nichiren, this Buddhist organization centers its practice on chanting a specific mantra — what is it?
Soka Gakkai: Japanese Buddhist religious movement.
He founded a Korean new religious movement known for mass 'Blessing' wedding ceremonies, and also launched an international news company behind The Washington Times — who was this messiah claimant?
Sun Myung Moon: Korean religious leader (1920–2012)
Launched as a surprise strike during the Lunar New Year — when most South Vietnamese troops were on leave — this 1968 campaign became one of the Vietnam War's largest. What was it?
Tet Offensive: 1968 Vietnam War military campaign. The Tet Offensive was both a major escalation and one of the largest military campaigns of the Vietnam War.
The military government of Japan from 1603 to 1868, established after the Battle of Sekigahara and based in Edo Castle—what is this shogunate called?
Tokugawa shogunate: 1603–1868 Japanese military government (Edo Jidai)

Exemplified by thinkers like Saint-Simon, Fourier, and Robert Owen, this early-19th-century current imagined ideal, non-capitalist societies but was later dismissed by Marxists as impractical — what is it called?
Utopian socialism: Political theory concerned with imagined socialist societies.
This Ukrainian-born Russian military blogger and convicted bank robber, who became a pro-war propagandist, was assassinated in a Saint Petersburg bombing in April 2023 — who was he?

Vladlen Tatarsky: Russian military blogger (1982–2023). Tatarsky was active as a propagandist for Russia and the separatist forces in Ukraine until he was assassinated in a bombing in Saint Petersburg in April 2023.

After nine years as a CIA clandestine officer, this politician represented a sprawling 550-mile Texas border district in Congress before mounting a brief 2024 presidential bid and endorsing Nikki Haley — who is he?
Founded by Grigory Yavlinsky and translating to 'Apple' in Russian, this social-liberal party held seats in the State Duma before losing its faction status in 2003 — which party?
Yabloko: Russian political party. The party consequently participated in the elections of deputies of the State Duma of the Federal Assembly of the Russian Federation of all eight convocations.
Mentioned in the Book of Exodus as the wife of Moses and daughter of the Midianite priest Jethro, this woman was the mother of Moses' two sons — who is she?
Which of these people was born first?
Benjamin Banneker (born 1731) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four. Thomas Carlyle (4 December 1795 – 5 February 1881) was a Scottish essayist, historian and philosopher.
Which of these four is the oldest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Joseph Henry is a physicist. Joseph Henry (December 17, 1797– May 13, 1878) was an American physicist and inventor who served as the first secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
What is the atomic number of Roentgenium?
Roentgenium (German: [ʁœntˈɡeːni̯ʊm]) is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
What is the atomic number of Mercury?
Mercury is a chemical element; it has symbol Hg and atomic number 80.
In what year was Claudine Gay born?
Claudine Gay (born August 4, 1970) is an American political scientist who is the Wilbur A.
In what year was Louis Pasteur born?
Louis Pasteur: Pasteur's works are credited with saving millions of lives through the developments of vaccines for rabies and anthrax.
In what year was Isaac Newton born?
Isaac Newton: Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.
In what year did Alexander Fleming die?
Alexander Fleming: Sir Alexander Fleming (6 August 1881 – 11 March 1955) was a Scottish physician and microbiologist.
In what year did John Maynard Keynes die?
John Maynard Keynes: Keynes was educated at King's College at the University of Cambridge, where he graduated in 1904 with a B.A. in mathematics.
In what year was Iron discovered?
Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Aero L-39 Albatros from?
Aero L-39 Albatros: Czechoslovakia. The Aero L-39 Albatros is a high-performance jet trainer designed and produced by Aero Vodochody in the Czech Republic.
Who is credited with discovering Caelum?
Caelum: Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. Caelum SEE-ləm is a faint constellation in the southern sky, introduced in the 1750s by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille and counted among the 88 modern constellations.
Who is credited with discovering 243 Ida?
243 Ida: Johann Palisa. 243 Ida is an asteroid in the Koronis family of the asteroid belt.
Who is credited with discovering Gliese 581d?
Gliese 581d: Stéphane Udry. It was the third planet claimed in the system and the fourth (in a 4-planet model) or fifth (in a disproven 5- or 6-planet model) in order from the star.
Who is credited with discovering Chlorofluorocarbon?
Chlorofluorocarbon: Frédéric Swarts. The most common example of a CFC is dichlorodifluoromethane (R-12).

This Scottish physician's 1928 discovery of a mould-derived substance later named benzylpenicillin has been called the single greatest victory ever achieved over disease, and earned him a shared Nobel Prize in 1945 — who is he?
Alexander Fleming (6 August 1881 - 11 March 1955) was a Scottish physician and microbiologist.
This unit of length equals one ten-billionth of a meter, or 100 picometres, and is named after a 19th-century Swedish physicist — what is it?
Angstrom (ONG-) is a unit of length equal to 1010 m; that is, one ten-billionth of a metre, a hundred-millionth of a centimetre, 0.1 nanometre, or 100 picometres.
Founder of a prominent Russian design studio and an avid, famously foul-mouthed blogger, this designer and entrepreneur is also a member of the Tolstoy family — name this designer?
Artemy Lebedev (born 13 February 1975) is a Russian designer, entrepreneur and Internet personality.
These nocturnal blood-feeding insects from the genus Cimex can trigger skin rashes, itching, and even psychological distress from their bites — what are they commonly called?
Bed bug are insects from the genus Cimex, which are parasites that feed on blood, usually at night.
Composed mostly of plasma along with red cells, white cells, and platelets, this body fluid ferries oxygen and nutrients to cells while hauling waste away — name the fluid?

Blood is a body fluid in the circulatory system of humans and other vertebrates that delivers necessary substances such as nutrients and oxygen to the cells of the body, and transports metabolic waste products away from those same cells.
The only living group in its tribe, this genus of over 250 fuzzy bees forms small colonies under a single queen — and unlike honeybees, its females can sting again and again — what is it?
Bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.

This quaternary ammonium compound ferries long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria for energy production, and is concentrated in heart and skeletal muscle, though most people synthesize enough on their own. What is it called?
Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants, and some bacteria.
Often preceded by a gallbladder attack and typically caused by a gallstone lodging in the cystic duct, which condition can progress to complications like gallstone pancreatitis?
Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder. Often gallbladder attacks (biliary colic) precede acute cholecystitis.
Native to Asia but so invasive in Australian cities that it was dubbed 'Most Important Pest/Problem' in 2008, which urban-adapted bird species is this?
Common myna (Acridotheres tristis), sometimes spelled mynah, is a bird in the family Sturnidae, native to Asia.
A bright yellow polyphenol found in turmeric, a member of the ginger family, this compound is sold as an herbal supplement, cosmetic ingredient, food flavoring, and food coloring — which compound?
Curcumin is a bright yellow chemical produced by the plant species Curcuma longa.

Occurring five times in the phrase 'no highway cowboys,' this linguistic term describes two vowel sounds gliding together within a single syllable, contrasting with a single steady vowel sound — what is it?
Diphthong (DIP-), also known as a gliding vowel or a vowel glide, is a combination of two adjacent vowel sounds within the same syllable.
Discovered to have two undescribed relatives only in 2019, this Amazonian 'knifefish' is best known for generating powerful electric discharges — which species?
Electrophorus electricus is the best-known species of electric eel. It is considered as a freshwater teleost which contains an electrogenic tissue that produces electric discharges.

This genus of 700-plus flowering trees gets its name from Greek words meaning 'well covered' — a nod to the little cap fused over its stamens — and most species are native to Australia. The leafy 'gum trees' in question are which?
Eucalyptus is a genus of more than 700 species of flowering plants in the family Myrtaceae.
Encompassing everything from oral tales and proverbs to festival rituals and traditional building styles, what term describes the shared expressive culture of a group?
Folklore is the body of expressive culture shared by a particular group of people, culture or subculture.
Ordained a priest in 1923, this Belgian physicist connected an expanding universe to Einstein's field equations and floated an early Big Bang hypothesis — who was he?
Georges Lemaître (lə-MET-rə; 17 July 1894 - 20 June 1966) was a Belgian Catholic priest, theoretical physicist, and mathematician who made major contributions to cosmology and astrophysics.

This small, hardy aquarium fish native to northeast South America gives birth to live young rather than laying eggs, and now ranks among the world's most widely kept tropical species — what fish is it?
Guppy (Poecilia reticulata), also known as the millionfish or rainbow fish, is a member of the family Poeciliidae and, akin to most New World members of the family, is classified as a livebearer.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

This phenomenon describes how a system's state depends on its history, as when a magnet holds different moments depending on past field changes — it underlies memory in a hard disk drive. What is it called?
Hysteresis is the dependence of the state of a system on its history. Hysteresis can be found in physics, chemistry, engineering, biology, and economics.

This English mathematician made foundational contributions to matrix and invariant theory, founded the American Journal of Mathematics at Johns Hopkins, and was teaching at Oxford when he died. Who was he?
James Joseph Sylvester (3 September 1814 - 15 March 1897) was an English mathematician.
Honored across Asia as a model healer and "Medicine King," this 5th-century BCE physician of Rajgir tended to King Bimbisāra — and to the Buddha himself. Who was he?
Jīvaka was the personal physician of the Buddha and the Indian King Bimbisra.
Native to the Mediterranean and prized for its fragrant purple blooms, this genus of some 47 flowering plant species belongs to the sage family — name it?
Lavandula (common name lavender) is a genus of 47 known species of perennial flowering plants in the sage family, Lamiaceae.

This American single-engine supersonic interceptor, designed by Kelly Johnson after interviewing Korean War fighter pilots, became part of the 'Century Series' and was widely used as a Cold War fighter-bomber. What is it?
Lockheed F-104 Starfighter is an American single-engine, supersonic interceptor. It was also produced under license by other nations and saw widespread service outside the United States.
A large canine of South America resembling a red fox in markings but being neither fox nor wolf. It's the only species in its genus and the largest canine in South America. What is it?
Maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus) is a large canine of South America.
Aristotle called this the 'first philosophy' — the branch that probes the most fundamental structure of reality, from existence itself to the categories of being — what is it?
Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that examines the basic nature or most fundamental structure of reality.
Found naturally in the dark resin of opium and given everywhere from pills to spinal injections, this opiate alters how the brain feels pain — what is it?
Morphine is an opiate found naturally in opium, a dark brown resin produced by drying the latex of opium poppies (Papaver somniferum).
This multidisciplinary field studies the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves — their function and their disorders — blending physiology, anatomy, and more — name the field?
Neuroscience is the scientific study of the nervous system (the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system), its functions, and its disorders.
Beginning in the embryo and maturing a primary oocyte into a fertilization-ready egg cell, what is this reproductive process called?
Oogenesis is the differentiation of the ovum (egg cell) into a cell competent to further develop when fertilized.
Named for the extra copy of chromosome 13 found in affected cells, this condition — related to Down and Edwards syndromes — disrupts normal organ development — which syndrome?
Patau syndrome is a syndrome caused by a chromosomal abnormality, in which some or all of the cells of the body contain extra genetic material from chromosome 13.
Prized as an ornamental indoor plant and still poorly understood taxonomically, this arum-family genus ranks second in size only to Anthurium — which genus?
Philodendron is a large genus of flowering plants in the family Araceae.
This category of polymer includes both natural proteins like wool and silk, and synthetic materials like nylon and aramid fibers — what is it?
Polyamide is a polymer with repeating units linked by amide bonds.
This noncontagious autoimmune condition leaves dry, scaly patches of skin and can flare at the exact spot of an injury — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon; what is it?
Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.
This rapidly worsening brain condition can follow a bout of chickenpox or influenza and is strongly associated with aspirin use in children — what syndrome is it?
Reye syndrome is a rapidly worsening brain disease. Signs and symptoms of Reye syndrome may include vomiting, personality changes, confusion, seizures, and loss of consciousness.
Named for the Latin word for willow tree, from which it was first derived, this plant hormone is both a precursor to aspirin and a common ingredient in anti-acne skincare — which compound?
Salicylic acid is an organic compound with the formula C7H6O3.

Essentially plasma with the clotting factors and cells removed, this pale yellow fluid still carries antibodies, hormones, and electrolytes and is central to typing tests done before a transfusion — what is it?
Serum (blood) is the fluid and solvent component of blood which does not play a role in clotting.

This genus of about 60 evergreen flowering plant species, native to the tropical Americas and Southeast Asia, is commonly grown as a houseplant valued for its large leaves and elegant white blooms — what genus is it?
Spathiphyllum is a genus of about 60 species of monocotyledonous flowering plants in the family Araceae, native to tropical regions of the Americas and southeastern Asia.
A single-seat, twin-engine, supermaneuverable 4.5-generation fighter derived from the Su-27, it was relabeled from "Su-27M" after the Soviet collapse to court export buyers — which Russian jet?
Sukhoi Su-35 (NATO reporting name: Flanker-E/M, occasionally nicknamed "Super Flanker") is the designation for two improved derivatives of the Su-27 air superiority fighter.
This group of inherited blood disorders reduces the body's hemoglobin production, sometimes causing anemia, an enlarged spleen, and stunted growth in children — what condition is it?
Thalassemia are a group of inherited blood disorders that manifest as the production of reduced hemoglobin.
Not a single branch of the family of life but a strategy evolved over and over — a tall trunk and branches reaching for sunlight — describes which kind of perennial plant?
Tree is a perennial plant with an elongated stem, or trunk, usually supporting branches and leaves.
Regarded as the 'Father of the Indian space program,' this physicist and astronomer also helped develop nuclear power in India, earning the Padma Vibhushan posthumously — who is he?
Vikram Sarabhai (12 August 1919 - 30 December 1971) was an Indian physicist and astronomer who initiated space research and helped to develop nuclear power in India.

Extracted from birch wood and named for the Greek word for 'wood', this white crystalline sugar alcohol is more soluble in water than any other common sugar alcohol except sorbitol. Name the compound?
Xylitol is an organic compound with the formula HOCH(CH(OH)CH2OH)2.
Caused by a mutation in the FGFR3 gene, this genetic disorder is the most common cause of short stature, marked by shortened limbs, a normal-length torso and a prominent forehead — what is it called?
Achondroplasia: Genetic condition, the most common form of dwarfism.
With wingspans reaching up to eleven and a half feet, which large seabird family ranges across the Southern Ocean and North Pacific but is absent from the North Atlantic?
Albatross: Family of large seabirds. The albatrosses are usually regarded as falling into four genera, but disagreement exists over the number of species.
Also known as shadbush, serviceberry, or juneberry, this rose-family shrub's berries inspired the name of a Canadian city — which genus?

Named from Greek words meaning "unlike other shrimp," this extinct arthropod from the Burgess Shale had swimming flaps, big compound eyes and grasping frontal appendages, reaching over a foot long — which prehistoric predator?
Anomalocaris: Extinct genus of cambrian radiodont.

Known only from fragmentary remains including vertebrae and a giant femur first found by a farmer in 1987, this titanosaur may be the largest land animal ever discovered, stretching up to 35 meters — which genus?
Argentinosaurus: Late Cretaceous giant sauropod dinosaur genus.

Despite its name being something of a misnomer, this herding dog breed was developed in California and takes its name from imported collies that arrived alongside sheep from Down Under — what breed is it?
Australian Shepherd: American breed of dog. The Australian Shepherd, also known as the Aussie, is a breed of herding dog from the United States.
Making up nearly 40% of all known insects with around 400,000 described species, this order is distinguished by front wings hardened into protective cases called elytra — what creatures are these?
Beetle: Order of insects. Over 300 species are used as food, mostly as larvae; species widely consumed include mealworms and rhinoceros beetle larvae.
This flowering vine's dried fruit is one of the most commonly traded spices in the world, its heat coming from a compound called piperine — what plant?
Black pepper: Ground fruit of the family Piperaceae.

Commonly known as mad cow disease, this fatal neurodegenerative illness in cattle is caused by a misfolded prion and can spread to humans as a variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. What is this cattle disease called?
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy: Fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle. The United Kingdom was afflicted with an outbreak of BSE and vCJD in the 1980s and 1990s.
Jointly developed by Pakistan and China as a lightweight fourth-generation fighter meant to eventually succeed the F-16 in Pakistan's air force, this jet's Chinese designation is FC-1 — what is it?
CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: Sino-Pakistani multirole fighter aircraft.
This medical emergency occurs when the heart suddenly stops beating effectively, cutting off blood flow to the brain and other organs within minutes — what is it called?
Cardiac arrest: Sudden or unexpected loss of heartbeat.
Latin for 'little brain,' this hindbrain structure fine-tunes motor coordination and timing without actually initiating movement — what is it?
Cerebellum: Structure at the rear of the vertebrate brain, beneath the cerebrum.
Every animal cell makes this waxy sterol — the liver most of all — and it doubles as the raw material for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. What is it?
Cholesterol: Sterol biosynthesized by all animal cells.
This scale insect that feeds on prickly pear cacti produces carminic acid, the basis of the red dye carmine used in lipstick and food coloring — what is it?
Cochineal: Species of insect producing the crimson dye carmine.
Known historically as blue vitriol, this bright blue crystalline compound with the formula CuSO4 forms an octahedral complex when dissolved in water — what compound?
Copper(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. It forms hydrates CuSO4·nH2O, where n can range from 1 to 7.

Named from the Greek for "dark blue," this compound's signature group is a carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen — and its soluble salts, like the potassium and sodium versions, are infamously deadly. What is it?
Cyanide: Any molecule with a cyano group (C≡N)
Working alongside longtime colleague Ken Thompson, this American computer scientist co-created the Unix operating system and the C programming language — who is he?
Dennis Ritchie: American computer scientist known for Unix (1941–2011)
Made from a fermented batter of rice and black gram, which thin, savoury South Indian flatbread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar?
Dosa (food): Thin batter bread originating from South India.
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints and stretchy, velvety skin, with a classification last updated in 2017 — what condition is it?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders. The existing classification was last updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms of EDS were added.
Despite never earning a university degree, this German-American psychoanalyst taught at Harvard, Berkeley, and Yale, and coined the term 'identity crisis' — who is he?
Erik Erikson: American psychoanalyst and essayist (1902–1994)

With a red face, a black-and-white head, and a bold yellow wing bar, this small finch native to the Palearctic often appears in Italian Renaissance paintings of the Madonna and Child. What bird is it?
European goldfinch: Species of bird. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.
Known as the weeping fig and the official tree of Bangkok, this flowering plant native to Asia and Australia is often used as a biomonitor in cities — which species?
Ficus benjamina: Species of fig. The species is also naturalized in the West Indies and in the states of Florida and Arizona in the United States.
Before becoming Ferrari's Formula One team principal in 2023, this Frenchman co-founded a junior-racing outfit that won back-to-back titles with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg — who is he?
Dubbed "the Godfather of AI" for his pioneering work on neural networks, this Nobel laureate quit Google in 2023 to warn about AI's risks. Who is he?
Caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and colloquially called 'the clap,' this sexually transmitted infection can pass from mother to child during birth — what is it?
Gonorrhea: Sexually transmitted infection. Gonorrhea or gonorrhoea, colloquially known as the clap, is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
This North Atlantic member of the true cod family is prized smoked as Finnan haddie or the Arbroath smokie — what fish is it?
Haddock: Species of fish. The haddock (Melanogrammus aeglefinus) is a saltwater ray-finned fish from the family Gadidae, the true cods.
This natural anticoagulant boosts the activity of antithrombin and is used to prevent clotting during dialysis and in blood test tubes — what medication is it?
Heparin: Anticoagulant. Heparin, also known as unfractionated heparin (UFH), is a medication and naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan.

This American physicist dared to drop the wave-function-collapse postulate, proposing a 'relative state' theory that became the basis of the many-worlds interpretation — largely ignored until quantum decoherence vindicated him. Who is he?
Known as 'the father of modern optics,' this Islamic Golden Age scholar wrote the influential 'Book of Optics' and proved that vision begins in the eye, not by rays leaving it — who is he?
Ibn al-Haytham: Arab physicist, mathematician and astronomer (c. 965 – c. 1040)
Awarded the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics, this British scientist discovered in 1897 that cathode rays were made of what we now call electrons — who is he?

This American physicist worked with Niels Bohr on nuclear fission and had a gift for coinages — "quantum foam," "wormhole," and the term that popularized "gravitationally collapsed objects." Who was he?
John Archibald Wheeler: American theoretical physicist (1911–2008)
Named from a Tongan and Marquesan word meaning 'bitter,' this pepper-family plant's ground root becomes a ceremonial Pacific Islands drink that numbs the mouth — what is it?
Kava: Species of plant. Kava or kava kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
Commonly called the voice box, which organ in the upper neck houses the vocal cords and protects the windpipe from food entering it?
Larynx: Voice box, an organ in the neck of amphibians, reptiles, and mammals.
The only person ever to win two unshared Nobel Prizes, this American chemist earned one for his work on the chemical bond and another for peace activism — who is he?
Linus Pauling: American scientist and activist (1901–1994)
This American experimental physicist won the 1968 Nobel Prize for discovering resonance states using the hydrogen bubble chamber — who was he?
Luis Walter Alvarez: American physicist, inventor and professor (1911–1988)

Often called the mirror image of depression, this psychiatric state brings racing thoughts, pressured speech, boundless energy, and a shrinking need for sleep — what is this elevated mood syndrome called?
Mania: State of abnormally elevated or irritable mood, arousal, and/or energy levels.
Developing from pigment-producing skin cells and most common on the legs in women and the back in men, about 30% of cases of this cancer arise from existing moles — what is it?
Melanoma: Skin cancer originating in melanocytes.
What is this — “Antiprogestogen and antiglucocorticoid drug”?
Mifepristone: Antiprogestogen and antiglucocorticoid drug. It is also used on its own to treat Cushing's syndrome or in low doses as an emergency contraceptive.
Native to tropical Central and South America, this genus of 59 flowering plant species belongs to the arum family — which genus?

The first production helicopter with fully fly-by-wire flight controls, this European twin-engine military chopper comes in troop-transport and naval anti-submarine variants flown by over a dozen NATO nations. What is it?
NHIndustries NH90: Family of military helicopters.
Surrounded by a typically darker-colored areola, this raised region of breast tissue is where milk exits through the lactiferous ducts during lactation — what is it?
Nipple: Part of the breast. The milk can flow through the nipple passively, or it can be ejected by smooth muscle contractions that occur along with the ductal system.
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz and built an early radio receiver he named the "coherer" — who was he?
Oliver Lodge: English physicist and electrical engineer (1851–1940)
Discovered in 1802 and named after a newly found asteroid, this silvery-white platinum-group metal is prized for cleaning up automobile exhaust in catalytic converters — which element?
Palladium: Chemical element with atomic number 46 (Pd)
Often described simply as the act of teaching, this discipline studies how knowledge and skills are imparted — and how that process shapes learners socially and psychologically. What is it?
Pedagogy: Theory and practice of education.
This branch of linguistics studies how speech sounds are articulated, transmitted as sound waves, and perceived, split into three sub-disciplines — what field is it?
Phonetics: Study of how humans produce and perceive sounds.
Sometimes called a 'collapsed lung,' this condition involves air trapped in the space between the lung and chest wall, causing sudden sharp one-sided chest pain — what is it?
Pneumothorax: Abnormal collection of air in the pleural space.
Manufactured in a soybean-oil emulsion that gives it a milky white look, this IV anesthetic — sold as Diprivan — induces unconsciousness fast and lets patients wake quickly; what is it?
Propofol: Intravenous medication used in anesthesia.
Guided by empiricist and positivist philosophy, which academic methodology turns data collection into numbers to test theories across the natural, applied, formal, and social sciences?
Quantitative research: All procedures for the numerical representation of empirical facts.
Found in grape skins and produced by plants as a defense against injury or infection, this compound is touted as a longevity supplement despite scant evidence it helps — what is it?
Resveratrol: Polyphenol with a stilbene skeleton.
Operating under the alias 'Dread Pirate Roberts,' this American created and ran the dark-web marketplace Silk Road until his 2013 FBI arrest — who is he?
Ross Ulbricht: American cybercriminal founder of Silk Road (born 1984)

Sometimes nicknamed the "seven-year itch," this contagious infestation by a tiny burrowing mite spreads fastest in crowded places and announces itself with fierce itching and a pimple-like rash — what is it?
This Pakistani-American billionaire owns an NFL franchise and a Premier League club, made his fortune supplying auto parts, and backs a wrestling promotion run by his son — who is he?
Shahid Khan: Pakistani and American businessman (born 1950)
Brittle, translucent, and found in nature as the mineral halite, this 1:1 compound seasons your fries and de-ices your roads. What is it?
Sodium chloride: Chemical compound with formula NaCl.
The most extreme form of malnutrition — a calorie deficit too deep to sustain life, sometimes wielded as a weapon and a crime under international law — goes by what name?
Starvation: Caloric intake below what is needed to maintain an organism's life.
Also called the broadbill, this large migratory predator sports a long, flat, pointed bill and can reach nearly 15 feet in length — what fish is it?
Swordfish: Fish which has a long, pointed bill. Swordfish are elongated, round-bodied, and lose all teeth and scales by adulthood.

Believing he'd been commanded to build the biblical Third Temple, this engineer single-handedly created an operating system written in a language he invented himself, despite later struggles with schizophrenia and homelessness — who was he?
Terry A. Davis: American computer programmer (1969–2018)
He joined Apple in 1998 to run worldwide operations and stepped up to the top job in 2011 when Steve Jobs resigned — which executive now leads the company?

Endemic to New Zealand and often mistaken for a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that thrived back in the Mesozoic era — its Māori name means 'peaks on the back.' What is it?
Tuatara: Species of reptile. The tuatara (Māori: [ˈtʉ.a.ta.ɾa]; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.
Found in Central and South America, only three living species of this blood-feeding, leaf-nosed flying mammal exist, while two extinct relatives once roamed North America — which creature?
Also known as ash pumpkin or winter melon, this South and Southeast Asian plant is grown for its very large fruit, eaten as a vegetable once mature — which plant?
Wax gourd: Species of vine and edible fruit.
Known to TV audiences as 'Dr. Now,' this Iranian-born American surgeon has spent over a decade helping patients on My 600-lb Life reach life-saving weight loss — who is he?
Younan Nowzaradan: Iranian-American surgeon, television personality, and author (born 1944)
Which of these four measures longest?
